pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📐 **Strand 3 — Geometry And Measurement**
Shape, space, measurement, position and movement — the mathematics of the world around us.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B8.3.1)
- B8.3.1.2 — Demonstrate the ability to perform geometric constructions of the angles 75°, 105°, 60°, 135° and 150°, construct triangles, and find the locus of points under given conditions.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- construct and bisect angles of 120°, 105°, 135° and 150°
- construct equilateral, isosceles, scalene, acute-angled, right-angled and obtuse-angled triangles under given conditions
- construct the locus of points: a fixed distance from a point; equidistant from two points; equidistant from two intersecting lines; equidistant from two parallel lines
- locate the centre of a circle and construct regular hexagons

pages.title: Constructing angles of 120°, 150°, 135° and 105°
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Construct and bisect angles of 120°, 105°, 135° and 150°.
Curriculum indicator B8.3.1.2.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Building angles from 60° and 90°** — 120° = 60° + 60° (or 180° − 60°); 150° = 120° + 30° (or 180° − 30°); 135° = 90° + 45° (or 180° − 45°); 105° = 90° + 15° (or 60° + 45°).
## ✏️ Example 9.1
Construct ∠CBA = 120° and confirm with a protractor.
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f26]]
Figure 9.1: Constructing 120° at B
1. Draw a line BC. With centre B and a convenient radius, draw a semicircle cutting BC at Q.
2. With centre Q and the same radius, mark R on the arc (∠QBR = 60°).
3. With centre R and the same radius, mark P on the arc (∠RBP = 60°).
4. Join BP and extend to A. ∠CBA = 60° + 60° = **120°**.
## ✏️ Example 9.2
Construct ∠SQC = 150°.
**Solution**
Construct 120° as above; then bisect the 60° angle between the 120° arm and the line on the other side (the angle ∠ABD where D is on CB produced). The bisector makes 120° + 30° = **150°** with QC. (Alternatively construct 30° on one side and use 180° − 30° = 150°.)
## ✏️ Example 9.3
Construct ∠ABC = 135°.
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f27]]
Figure 9.2: 135° = 90° + 45°
1. Draw a straight line through B. Construct a perpendicular BD at B (90°).
2. Bisect the right angle on the far side (∠DBE = 90°) to get 45°.
3. ∠ABC = 90° + 45° = **135°**.

pages.title: Example 9.4
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 9.4
Construct an angle of 105° and verify with a protractor.
**Solution**
Construct a perpendicular at B (90°). On the other side of the perpendicular, construct 30° (bisect 60°) and bisect that to get 15°. Then 90° + 15° = **105°**. (Or: construct 120° and 90° at the same point and bisect the 30° between them: 90° + 15° = 105°.)

pages.title: Constructing triangles
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Construct scalene, isosceles, equilateral, obtuse-angled and acute-angled triangles in different orientations under given conditions.
Curriculum indicator B8.3.1.2.2
## ✏️ Example 9.5
Construct an equilateral triangle VJN with side VJ = 6.2 cm. Justify that it is equilateral.
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f28]]
Figure 9.3: Equilateral triangle VJN
1. Draw VJ = 6.2 cm.
2. With centre V and radius 6.2 cm, draw an arc. With centre J and the same radius, draw an arc to cut the first at N.
3. Join VN and JN.
VN = JN = VJ = 6.2 cm because all three were drawn with the same radius, so the triangle is **equilateral**. Each angle measures 60° (check with a protractor).
## ✏️ Example 9.6
Construct an isosceles right-angled triangle on a base line AB = 5 cm (right angle at A).
**Solution**
Construct a perpendicular AD at A. Mark C on AD with AC = 5 cm (an arc of radius 5 cm from A). Join BC. Then AB = AC, ∠A = 90° and ∠B = ∠C = 45°.
## ✏️ Example 9.7
Construct triangle LMN with LM = 6 cm, LN = 8 cm and MN = 7 cm.
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f29]]
Figure 9.4: Triangle with three sides given
1. Draw LM = 6 cm.
2. With centre L and radius 8 cm, draw an arc.
3. With centre M and radius 7 cm, draw an arc to cut the first arc at N.
4. Join LN and MN. Triangle LMN is the required (scalene) triangle.

pages.title: Example 9.8
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 9.8
Construct an isosceles triangle with base BC = 7 cm and base angles of 30°. Construct an acute-angled triangle PQR with QR = 8 cm, ∠Q = 60° and ∠R = 45°.
**Solution**
Isosceles: draw BC = 7 cm; construct 30° at B and at C (bisect 60°); the arms meet at A. AB = AC.
Acute-angled: draw QR = 8 cm; construct 60° at Q and 45° at R; the arms meet at P. ∠P = 180° − 60° − 45° = 75°, so all angles are acute.
## ✏️ Example 9.9
Construct triangle ABC in which AC = 3 cm, AB = 5 cm and ∠CAB = 45° (two sides and the included angle).
**Solution**
Draw AB = 5 cm. Construct ∠BAD = 45° at A. Mark C on AD so that AC = 3 cm. Join BC and measure it (≈ 3.6 cm).
> 🎯 **BECE tip** Always draw a **rough sketch** first, labelled with the given measurements. It shows you where to start and which construction to use at each vertex.

pages.title: Loci
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Construct loci under given conditions: from a fixed point; equidistant from two fixed points; equidistant from two intersecting straight lines; equidistant from two parallel lines.
Curriculum indicator B8.3.1.2.3
> 🔑 **Key idea: Locus** — A **locus** (plural **loci**) is the set of all points (or the path of a point) that obey a given rule.
[[fig:m8-f30|Figure 9.5: The four basic loci]]
| **Rule** | **Locus** |
|---|---|
| A fixed distance r from a fixed point O | a **circle** with centre O and radius r |
| Equidistant from two fixed points A and B | the **perpendicular bisector** (mediator) of AB |
| Equidistant from two intersecting lines | the **bisectors of the angles** between the lines |
| Equidistant from two parallel lines | a **parallel line midway** between them |
| A fixed distance d from a straight line | **two parallel lines**, one on each side, at distance d |
## ✏️ Example 9.10
Describe the locus of a point P which moves so that its distance from a fixed point O is always 3 cm.
**Solution**
P traces a **circle with centre O and radius 3 cm**. A goat tied to a peg with a 3 m rope can graze up to the circle of radius 3 m.
## ✏️ Example 9.11
Explain why the perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B.
**Solution**
Construct the perpendicular bisector CD of AB, with midpoint M. Take any point P on CD. Triangles PMA and PMB have PM common, AM = MB and ∠PMA = ∠PMB = 90°, so they are congruent and **PA = PB**. Every point on CD is the same distance from A and B — and no point off the line is. So CD is the locus. (In the construction, the arc intersections C and D are themselves equidistant from A and B because equal radii were used.)

pages.title: Example 9.12
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 9.12
Locate the centre of a circle.
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f31]]
Figure 9.6: The perpendicular bisectors of two chords meet at the centre
Draw any two chords AB and CD. Construct the perpendicular bisector of each. The centre is equidistant from all points on the circle, so it lies on both bisectors: their **intersection O is the centre**.
## ✏️ Example 9.13
Construct the angle bisector as the locus of points equidistant from two lines that meet, and explain why.
**Solution**
Bisect the angle between the lines. From any point P on the bisector, drop perpendiculars PX and PY to the two lines. Triangles PXO and PYO are congruent (common side OP, equal angles at O, right angles at X and Y), so **PX = PY**: every point on the bisector is the same distance from both lines.
## ✏️ Example 9.14
Construct the locus of a point P that moves so that it is always 2 cm from a line BC. Then show that two given lines AB and CD are parallel.
**Solution**
At several points on BC construct perpendiculars and mark points 2 cm away on each side. Join them: the locus is **two lines parallel to BC**, each 2 cm away.
To show AB ∥ CD: mark three points P, Q and R on AB; construct perpendiculars from them to meet CD at E, F and G. Measure PE, QF and RG. If they are all equal, the lines are parallel — **the perpendicular distance between parallel lines is the same everywhere**.

pages.title: Circles and regular hexagons
pages.body:
## Circles and regular hexagons
## ✏️ Example 9.15
Construct a regular hexagon ABCDEF with |AB| = 6 cm, in a circle. Measure ∠AOB (O the centre) and the interior angles. What do you observe?
**Solution**
[[fig:m8-f32]]
Figure 9.7: Regular hexagon in a circle of radius 6 cm
1. Draw a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm (the side of a regular hexagon equals the radius).
2. Mark A on the circle. With the compasses still open at 6 cm, step round the circle marking B, C, D, E and F.
3. Join A, B, C, D, E, F in order.
Observations: ∠AOB = 360° ÷ 6 = **60°** (triangle AOB is equilateral). Each interior angle (e.g. ∠ABC, ∠DEF) = **120°** = 2 × 60°.
## ✏️ Example 9.16
Use intersecting circles to construct a regular hexagon with |OA| = 5 cm.
**Solution**
Draw a circle centre O, radius 5 cm, and mark A on it. Draw a circle of radius 5 cm centred on A; it cuts the first circle at B and F. Draw circles of the same radius centred on B, then on C, and so on — each new circle cuts the first circle at the next vertex. Join the six points. All sides measure 5 cm and each interior angle is 120°.

pages.title: Exercise 9.3
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 9.3** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. Mark two points A and B 7 cm apart. Construct the locus of points equidistant from A and B. Mark a point P on it that is 5 cm from A. How far is P from B?
2. Draw two lines meeting at 70°. Construct the locus of points equidistant from them.
3. A goat is tied to a post with a rope 4 m long in an open field. Describe and sketch the region it can graze.
4. Draw two parallel lines 6 cm apart. Construct the locus of points equidistant from both.
5. Draw a circle of radius 4.5 cm without marking its centre (trace round a tin). Find its centre by construction.
6. Construct a regular hexagon of side 4 cm and measure the distance between opposite vertices.

pages.title: Chapter 9 summary
pages.body:
- Constructible angles come from 60° (equilateral triangle) and 90° (perpendicular) by adding and bisecting.
- A triangle can be constructed from: three sides; two sides and the included angle; one side and two angles.
- Loci: circle (fixed distance from a point), perpendicular bisector (equidistant from two points), angle bisector (equidistant from two lines), mid-parallel (equidistant from parallel lines).
- The side of a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle equals the radius.
